items.title: China’s property starts plunge to 2002 levels
items.original_title: China’s property starts plunge to 2002 levels
items.summary: China’s property construction collapse has taken new building starts back to levels last seen in 2002, raising fresh questions about the long-term outlook for iron ore and coking coal demand, even as dry bulk owners become increasingly bullish about freight markets. Research published today by Ursa Shipbrokers reveals that Chinese property starts have fallen by 74% since 2019, from 2.27bn sq m to just 588m sq m last year. The deterioration is continuing. In the first nine months of 2026, new starts totalled 340m sq m, down 25% year-on-year and almost 80% below the equivalent period in 2019. Ursa notes that although construction starts have returned to levels comparable with the early 2000s, the circumstances could scarcely be more different. Chinese iron ore imports actually increased 4.1% in the first nine months of 2026, reflecting greater reliance on overseas supplies, inventory accumulation and changing trade patterns. Dionysios Tsilioris, a researcher with Ursa, told Splash today that the historic link between Chinese property starts and capesize earnings has disconnected to a large degree. China’s traditional construction-led demand engine continues to deteriorate, but longer trading distances and shifting mineral supply chains are helping support freight markets. Whether those factors can continue offsetting China’s structural property slump is emerging as a central question for capesize owners.

items.title: The human breaking point at sea
items.original_title: The human breaking point at sea
items.summary: Shipping cannot keep demanding more from less, argues Steven Jones, the founder of the Seafarers Happiness Index, in this strident exclusive for Splash. We are entering an extraordinary era of maritime technology. AI, autonomous ships, digital twins and sensors promise to transform shipping. The index, drawing on seafarers’ own accounts, fell to 6.81/10 in Q3 from 6.87 in Q2, continuing a decline from 7.26 in the last quarter of 2025. When people become exceptionally good at coping, organisations and industries can become exceptionally comfortable with the conditions they endure. One Captain describes manageable workloads at sea, followed by cargo operations, inspections, regulatory requirements and paperwork converging in port, while the office presses for shorter turnarounds. The Seafarers Happiness Index describes extraordinary commitment, but that should not be allowed to reassure us too much. A system can appear successful precisely because the people within it are absorbing its failures. We cannot keep demanding more from less and assuming resilience will fill the gaps.

items.original_title: Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high despite attacks, Red Sea traffic also rises
items.summary: Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic rose to its highest monthly level since July in October, supported by stronger dry-bulk and LNG movements despite a decline in VLCC traffic and mounting regional threats, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data showed Nov. 2. The rise came amid an “increasingly volatile” operating environment at Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, with “reported projectile strikes, vessel fires and other security incidents” throughout October, CAS said. Despite elevated security risks over the month, observed and assumed Hormuz traffic totaled 750 transits in October, up from 749 in September, as VLCC traffic fell to 156 transits in October from 184 the previous month, but the declines in crude tanker transits were more than offset by other vessel classes, according to the CAS report. LNG carrier crossings, which fell steeply since Qatar LNG production units suffered damage at the start of the Iran war, also climbed, reaching 32 transits, or their highest since the start of the war. The Iranian authority had listed 240 vessels as violating its Strait of Hormuz transit guidelines and previously threatened non-compliant vessels with fines, seizure or confiscation. In the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab traffic rose to 1,196 transits in October from 1,154 in September, while tanker movements were stable at 408 versus 404, CAS reported.

Over the past four years, four additional Chinese shipyards—Jiangnan Shipyard, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry, Yangzijiang Shipyard, and China Merchants—have entered the LNG carrier market. items.title: Wärtsilä completes milestone marine sector project to reduce methane emissions on vessels

items.summary: Technology group Wärtsilä has successfully completed the conversion of one engine on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel (DF) to spark gas (SG) operation. This conversion aims to lower greenhouse gas emissions from the vessels by reducing methane slip, un-combusted methane that can escape into the atmosphere from LNG fuel. Following the successful conversion of these first three vessels, three additional vessel conversions are planned for execution later this year and next year, bringing the total number of converted vessels to six. This project represents a technical collaboration within the marine sector focused on addressing methane emissions from LNG-fueled vessels. items.title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
items.original_title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
items.summary: Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power , by far the highest proportion in the EU. These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

Boasting a 27% year-on-year revenue increase, Union Pacific took home some $1.52bn over the quarter, with volumes up 11%, to 956,000 carloads, and pointing specifically to reduced trucking capacity as behind the gains. “We’re very optimistic about the opportunities as we close this year and go into next on the domestic intermodal side,” she told investors, adding that the tightening in trucking could prove a boost when yields come up for renewal. Not one to miss out, Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) also reported double-digit revenue growth in intermodal, up 22% year on year to $583m, as volumes rose 9%, to 489,800 carloads. items.title: Norway Detains Sanctioned Chinese Vessel Over False Flag Registration
items.original_title: Norway Detains Sanctioned Chinese Vessel Over False Flag Registration
items.summary: Norway has detained a Chinese-owned heavy-lift vessel sanctioned for its role in delivering equipment to Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project, in what appears to be the first known detention in the Arctic of a Chinese vessel linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. The Ya Qing Hai Yang was detained after Norwegian inspectors found that it lacked valid flag-state registration and required certificates, the Norwegian Maritime Authority said. The case is a notable enforcement action against a vessel with documented ties to Russia’s sanctioned energy sector, although authorities say the detention was based on maritime safety and registration deficiencies rather than the ship’s sanctions status. “During the inspection, it was discovered that the vessel did not have a valid flag registration and lacked the required certificates,” Dag Inge Aarhus, the authority’s communications director said last week. “The vessel has therefore been detained until further notice.” The vessel remains off the Vesterålen Islands as of November 3. The ship must establish valid registration with a flag state and obtain the necessary certificates before Norwegian authorities can complete the inspection and consider its release. The detention appears to be the first publicly documented case of Norway holding a vessel sailing under an invalid flag registration. items.summary: Nov 3, 2026 (Bloomberg) –German startup Stark Defence plans to launch a 24-meter uncrewed surface vessel next year, marking an expansion beyond small drones to more closely resemble an established defense contractor. The Berlin-based company’s new ship is designed to guard undersea cables and track Russia’s shadow fleet in European waters, Stark’s Chief Executive Officer Uwe Horstmann announced at Bloomberg Tech London on Tuesday. “Those are systems that cost a thousandth of the price of a manned frigate, which takes years to produce,” Horstmann said. Stark plans to develop the Vanta 24 in the UK and Germany, and hired Stephen Brian, a former nuclear submarine commander for the British Royal Navy, to run the company’s naval operations. He described Vanta 24 as a versatile vessel designed to escort warships or surveil on its own, replacing the labor-intensive work of monitoring coastlines and subsea cables. In June, it reached a valuation of €3.2 billion ($3.6 billion) and has grown to more than 700 employees. Luciana Lixandru, a partner with Sequoia Capital, said the Silicon Valley investor backed Stark because it believes the company will be one of Europe’s few defense newcomers to compete with prime contractors.

items.summary: Concern is rising among cargo owners and logistics providers that a strike at the Los Angeles/Long Beach port complex could turbo-charge the congestion there. About 250 watchmen, who perform security-related duties at container terminals at the twin ports, are poised to walk off the job at 5pm Pacific time on Wednesday, should last-minute contract negotiations between the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) fail to reach agreement. Watchmen have been working under contract extensions since the agreement expired in July 2025. Union members had authorised a strike for 1 November, but both sides agreed to extend negotiations until 4 November. According to the PMA, a work stoppage would affect 85% of the container traffic at the port of Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles. Ted Chen, ocean freight and trade compliance director at logistics provider Dimerco, said there was a high likelihood that other port employees would support the strike, a concern echoed by forwarder Woodland Group. The actual scale of any interruption would depend on the terminals affected, the participation of other workers and the duration of industrial action.” ,Moreover, the disruption would aggravate congestion that has resulted in extended dwell times for rail cargo at several of the affected terminals.

items.original_title: Offshore operators should not wait for EU ETS clarity to act on emissions data
items.summary: EU MRV has applied to offshore vessels of 400 GT and above since 1 January 2025, and vessels of 5,000 GT and above are scheduled to enter the EU ETS from the 2027 reporting period. On 17 July 2026, the European Commission published proposals that would revise the MRV framework from 1 January 2029 and bring offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 GT into the ETS from 2031. These are not final, however, and must still pass through the legislative process. The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has welcomed the recognition of offshore-specific terminology and operational realities, but says more clarity is needed on ports of call, cross-border operations and how the EU and UK ETS interact. In August, Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment confirmed that FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation, previously expected to take effect later this year, will not enter into force for Norway before 1 January 2028. From 2029, companies operating on the Norwegian continental shelf must reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of ships used in oil and gas activity, starting at 10% for 2029-2031 and rising in stages to 40% for 2038-2040. Rystad Energy estimates close to 300 offshore vessels fall within scope, and that most of them, including LNG dual-fuel units, would miss the first threshold based on how they operate today.

items.title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
items.original_title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
items.summary: The cost of fuelling ships has climbed back above $1,000 a tonne in Singapore for the first time since March, as the prolonged Iran conflict continues to drive up bunker bills across the global merchant fleet. Data from Ship & Bunker show very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) broke through the $1,000 threshold on October 28, reaching $1,000.50 a tonne. Prices subsequently climbed to $1,019.50 on Friday before easing to $1,003.50 on Monday. Ship & Bunker data show Singapore VLSFO was trading at $521.50 a tonne immediately before the conflict. The fuel has since increased by more than 92%, having reached a peak of $1,120.50 on March 13. For a ship taking on 3,000 tonnes of VLSFO, the current bunker bill is approximately $3m, compared with $1.56m before the war, an additional $1.45m for a single stem. Scrubber-equipped vessels retain a significant advantage, with the Singapore VLSFO-HSFO spread currently standing at $105 a tonne. According to bunker pricing specialist ENGINE, LNG bunkers in Singapore reached $1,939 a tonne on Monday, up $74 over the previous week. Ship & Bunker assessed Rotterdam VLSFO at $763.50 a tonne on Monday, around $240 below Singapore, while Fujairah was quoted at $991.50.

items.title: When the ship pays back before the owner does
items.original_title: When the ship pays back before the owner does
items.summary: Fuel-saving retrofits can pay for themselves long before the shipowner who funded them sees a return. A new BIMCO contract seeks to resolve shipping’s longstanding divide between who pays for efficiency and who pockets the savings. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. If the owner pays to burn less, the immediate fuel saving shows up first in the charterer’s accounts. If the charterer pays, the steel stays on someone else’s ship when the fixture ends. If the owner funds the whole amount and keeps half of that saving, the owner’s simple payback stretches to about 4.9 years. Yet the owner would have recovered only $1.44m, leaving $910,000 still unrecovered when the fixture ended. The ship can reach payback before the investor does. Under BIMCO’s ETS clause for time charter, the charterer provides and pays for the allowances corresponding to the vessel’s emissions during the charter period.

items.original_title: Chinese ship-owner CMES holds vessel-naming ceremony in South Korea, advancing the two countries’ shipbuilding cooperation
items.summary: The first vessel under China Merchants Energy Shipping’s (CMES) second-phase LNG project with QatarEnergy was named in South Korea on October 28-29, according to media reports, marking progress in cooperation between Chinese ship-owners and South Korean shipbuilders. The LEKHRAIB, the first of six 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carriers ordered by CMES from South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), was named during ceremonies held on Geoje Island and in Busan. The vessel will provide long-term LNG transportation services for QatarEnergy. In addition to the six vessels built by Samsung Heavy Industries, CMES secured long-term transportation contracts for four larger 271,000-cubic-meter QC MAX carriers, which are being built by China’s Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding. LNG carriers are among the most technologically demanding commercial vessels, as they transport natural gas at temperatures of around minus 162 C. The LEKHRAIB features a GTT Mark III Flex membrane containment system, with a designed daily boil-off rate of no more than 0.085 percent, as well as dual-fuel engines. South Korean shipbuilders have long held a strong position in large LNG carrier construction, while Chinese shipyards have been expanding their capabilities and securing more orders for advanced vessels, Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times.

The vessels will have a single box-shaped cargo hold measuring more than 89 m in length, while a forward-mounted superstructure will provide additional deck space for oversized cargo. Asia Break Bulk, which marks its 20th anniversary this year, has traditionally operated semi-liner services connecting Asia and Europe. Maximilian Fischer, general manager at Asia Break Bulk, said customers are increasingly looking for shorter transit times and direct access to ports with draft restrictions, reducing the need for costly and time-consuming transshipments. Schoeller Holdings is backing the newbuilding programme, while Columbia Shipmanagement will supervise construction and take over technical and crew management once the vessels enter service. The deal adds another chapter to Cyprus-based Schoeller’s extensive investment in multipurpose and heavylift tonnage. Earlier this year, the group booked two 32,000 dwt MPP vessels at China’s CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding for delivery in 2029, extending a relationship with the yard dating back to 2008.

items.title: Russia moves to bar ageing foreign ships from its ports
items.original_title: Russia moves to bar ageing foreign ships from its ports
items.summary: Russia has formally put proposed restrictions on ageing merchant ships out for public consultation, seeking to bar foreign-flagged vessels older than 40 years from its ports as Moscow tightens oversight of the fleet carrying its seaborne trade. The transport ministry published the draft legislation, proposing a separate 50-year threshold for Russian-flagged ships, with transitional arrangements tied to the validity of their classification certificates. Foreign-flagged vessels older than 30 years would also face annual inspections to confirm compliance with safety and environmental requirements. The proposed rules would assess vessels against their inspection and repair records, technical condition and insurance coverage. Cargo transportation contracts would also have to specify the use of compliant ships, while marine terminal operators would assume additional responsibilities for ensuring vessels meet the requirements. The move advances an initiative Moscow has been developing for more than a year. The transport ministry outlined the proposed 40-year limit for foreign ships in July, alongside plans for tighter oversight of older Russian tonnage. However, the government faces a substantial fleet replacement challenge. Deputy transport minister Alexander Poshivay said last month that restrictions would not be adopted until the country was confident replacement vessels could be secured, acknowledging that domestic shipyards face constraints on capacity, pricing and construction times.

items.summary: Eight maritime associations including the Royal Belgian Shipowners’ Association (KBRV) send an open letter to EU policymakers urging them to ensure a fit-for-purpose framework for the European offshore sector under the current EU ETS review. The offshore shipping sector is a strategic asset to the European economy, playing a leading role in the continent’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness. Yet the current EU ETS framework, entering into force beginning 2027 for offshore vessels, will distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on a Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose. The sector strongly urges EU policymakers to first ensure that a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational, before the inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in EU ETS from next year onwards. Below is the open letter the sector has addressed to the European Parliament and members of the Council EU ETS REVIEW: GET THE FRAMEWORK RIGHT FOR EUROPE’S OFFSHORE SECTOR Open letter to Members of the European Parliament and EU Member States’ Permanent Representatives.

items.title: LNG Carrier Prices Fall to $245 Million, Threatening Korean Shipbuilders’ Margins
items.original_title: LNG Carrier Prices Fall to $245 Million, Threatening Korean Shipbuilders’ Margins
items.summary: Prices for high-value vessels, including liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers and ultra-large container ships, have begun to decline despite rising demand. Intensifying competition from Chinese shipbuilders entering the premium vessel market, coupled with their aggressive supply strategies, is putting downward pressure on newbuilding prices. According to UK-based shipping market intelligence provider Clarksons Research, the benchmark newbuilding price for an LNG carrier stood at $245 million as of Oct. Prices for ultra-large container ships also declined over the same period, from $266.5 million to approximately $242 million. The downturn is particularly notable given that LNG carrier orders have increased more than 4.5-fold year-on-year. Jiangnan Shipyard has also intensified price competition by securing LNG carrier orders at $225 million per vessel, undercutting prevailing benchmark prices and challenging South Korean shipbuilders’ market share. South Korean shipbuilders are unlikely to experience an immediate earnings impact, as this year’s results largely reflect vessels ordered at peak prices approximately two years ago. With shipping capacity expanding ahead of available cargo volumes, shipowners have less incentive to pay premium prices for new vessels. Industry experts say South Korean shipbuilders need to accelerate technological development and business diversification to maintain their competitive edge over Chinese rivals.

items.title: US suspends Chinese vessel port fees for 2 months, will accept public comment
items.original_title: US suspends Chinese vessel port fees for 2 months, will accept public comment
items.summary: The US Trade Representative (USTR) will take public comment through 30 October and is suspending the implementation of port fees for Chinese vessels by two months as officials from both countries continue to negotiate broader trade issues. The new fees were set to take effect on 10 November after the US and China agreed in November 2025 to suspend tit-for-tat maritime charges for one year as part of a broader trade agreement. They will now take effect on 9 January if no other agreement is reached. The temporary suspension means that no parties will accrue liability for, or be required to pay, the transport service fees or associated product duties during the extended window. The US initially targeted the fees for ships owned, operated, or built in China in October 2025, prompting China to enact similar charges for US-linked ships entering Chinese ports. The initial USTR proposal was published in February 2025 in the Federal Register and included proposed service fees of up to $1.5 million per US port call for vessels built in China, and up to $1 million per port call for China-based operators. The action was taken after a Section 301 investigation determined China’s acts, policies and practices to be unreasonable and to burden or restrict US commerce.

items.summary: Swiss marine power company WinGD has signed its first-ever license agreement with engine builder HD Hyundai Marine Engine (formerly STX Heavy Industries). HD Hyundai Marine Engine was acquired by HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, part of HD Hyundai Group, in 2024. Its expertise in small and mid-sized two-stroke engines complements the large engine specialism of HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, with which WinGD has a long-standing license agreement, and which delivers engines for large vessels including ultra-large container vessels and LNG carriers. WinGD Vice President Product Centre, Peter Krähenbühl was on hand for the signing and said: “This new agreement expands our ability to deliver main engines for high-volume vessel segments in Korea and enables HD Hyundai Marine Engine’s customers to select WinGD engine technology. We look forward to working closely with HD Hyundai Marine Engine to strengthen the availability and competitiveness of WinGD’s mid-bore engine portfolio .” Under the agreement, WinGD and HD Hyundai Marine Engine will share knowledge and experience to continue reducing the cost and improving vessel design integration of WinGD’s mid-bore engines, while safeguarding their high reliability and in-service performance.

items.title: Can carriers avoid overcapacity in 2027?
items.original_title: Can carriers avoid overcapacity in 2027?
items.summary: The backdrop is difficult to ignore. Around 5 mteu of new capacity has been ordered in each of the past three years, pushing the orderbook-to-fleet ratio to approximately 45%, its highest level since 2009. The orderbook is fast approaching 16 mteu, with September the second-busiest contracting month on record at 1.1 mteu, following major orders from the world’s two largest carriers: MSC (20 × 24,000 teu) and Maersk (20 × 18,600 teu). Ultimately, the 2027 outcome will depend on whether demand growth, slow steaming and congestion can absorb capacity faster than new ships enter service. Overcapacity is, in our view, unavoidable. More than 70% expect some degree of overcapacity in 2027, with 56.7% anticipating a moderate surplus and 14.2% predicting significant overcapacity. Blank sailings, service adjustments and other measures can help contain the surplus, but respondents appear unconvinced that carriers can fully offset the delivery pipeline. Cargo demand attracted just 11.7%, while demolitions accounted for only 1.3%, suggesting that neither stronger demand nor the removal of older tonnage is widely expected to be the decisive factor. Our view The poll reinforces our assessment that 2027 will be a test of carriers’ ability to manage a growing capacity surplus rather than prevent one altogether.

items.title: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
items.original_title: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
items.summary: A Taiwan Coast Guard patrol vessel moves in Keelung, as China conducts "Justice Mission 2025" military drills around Taiwan, in Keelung, Taiwan, December 30, 2025. REUTERS/Ann Wang TAIPEI, Nov 1 (Reuters) – China’s Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch. China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Taiwan’s Coast Guard said China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality.” “Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added. China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said separately. Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added.
